title: Sweating the Small Stuff
author: Laura Burke
summary: This article by a former headteacher argues that the difference between a good classroom and a great one is found not in dramatic pedagogical strategies or bold approaches but in hundreds of tiny acts of deliberate attention that compound over time. The author describes her signature leadership phrase — 'we sweat the small stuff' — as shorthand for a way of noticing and caring about classroom details that rarely appear in policies or improvement plans: which paper to model on, the pause before a question, the choice of which student to call on first and why, circulating with an intentional route. Burke argues that great teachers pay extraordinary attention to the ordinary because they understand that learning is fragile, attention is limited, and working memory is easily overwhelmed — making the specific details of what students look at, listen to, and think about at each moment critical to whether learning becomes possible or quietly slips away. The piece concludes that these habits compound across lessons and years, making incremental invisible improvements that reshape students' experience of learning in ways that grand strategies never can.
points: The difference between a good classroom and a great one is often invisible to anyone not looking for small things — it is found in hundreds of tiny acts of deliberate attention repeated daily, not in dramatic strategies or bold changes of approach.

Learning is fragile, attention is limited, and working memory is easily overwhelmed — which means the specific details of what students look at, listen to, and think about in each moment determine whether learning becomes possible or quietly slips away.

Great teachers pay extraordinary attention to the ordinary: which paper to model on, whether the pupil at the back can see properly, whether the explanation has gone on slightly too long, whether the example on the board is exactly as clear as it could be.

Small classroom details are not small at all — they are the mechanisms through which learning either becomes possible or quietly slips away, and their power is only visible to those who know what to look for.

These habits compound over time: a slightly clearer model, a slightly sharper explanation, a slightly better choice of example, a slightly more deliberate pause — individually trivial, but collectively reshaping how pupils experience learning across a whole year.
quotes: There is a phrase I used often with staff when I was a headteacher. We sweat the small stuff. At the time, it was shorthand for a way of working. A way of noticing. A way of caring about the details of classroom life that are easy to overlook because they appear too minor to matter.

Over time, I have come to believe that the difference between a good classroom and a great one is frequently invisible to anyone who is not looking for these small things. It is not usually found in dramatic strategies or bold changes of approach. It is found in hundreds of tiny acts of deliberate attention, repeated lesson after lesson, day after day.

Great teachers pay extraordinary attention to the ordinary. They notice when a pupil cannot quite see the modelling clearly and adjust their position. They are careful to use the same pen colour that pupils will use so that what is modelled is exactly what is expected.

This is not accidental. It comes from an understanding, sometimes instinctive and sometimes learned, that learning is fragile. Attention is limited. Working memory is easily overwhelmed. What pupils look at, listen to and think about in each moment matters enormously.
Because of this, small details are not small at all. They are the mechanisms through which learning either becomes possible or quietly slips away.

The teachers who make the most difference are rarely those who are thinking about grand ideas while they teach. They are thinking about whether the pupil at the back can see properly, whether the explanation has gone on for slightly too long, whether the example on the board is as clear as it could be, and whether pupils are attending to the right thing at the right time.
